growth_story.headline: Steady growth since 1990 on tourism and an open economy, broken by a 2003 bank crash and the pandemic, and cooling in recent years
growth_story.arc: The data show one long era since 1990: income per person grew 3.3 percent a year on average from 1990 to 2025, with no lasting shift up or down. After a fall of 7.4 percent in 1990, the IMF describes strong performance from 1992 to 2000; the run then faded and turned into a fall of 2.8 percent in 2003, the year a large private bank failed after fraud came to light. Growth came back by 2005, and the World Bank credits an open economy, a business-friendly setting, a strong tourism sector and steady policy for two decades of fast growth. The pandemic cut income per person by 8.9 percent in 2020, and the reopening, with tourists returning fast, brought a 12.8 percent rebound in 2021. Growth has cooled since then: 4.1 percent a year in 2006 to 2015, 3.3 percent in 2016 to 2025, and 1.3 percent in 2025 as high interest rates held back credit and building, though income per person still reached a new high of about 9,287 dollars (in constant prices) in 2025.

threads.title: Open economy, tourism, steady policy
threads.text: The World Bank links the country's long run of fast growth to an open economy, a business-friendly setting and a strong tourism sector. It also points to careful monetary and budget policy that kept prices stable and jobs growing.

threads.title: Pandemic fall and fast rebound
threads.text: The pandemic cut income per person by 8.9 percent in 2020. The IMF credits sound policy, a quick vaccine drive and a well-timed reopening for the recovery, and tourist arrivals passed their 2019 level from late 2021.

threads.title: Dear credit slows 2025
threads.text: From late 2024, tighter money worldwide and high interest rates at home cut lending, above all for homes. Building shrank, investment fell, and income per person grew only 1.3 percent in 2025.

since_last_year.text: Growth slipped in 2025, when income per person rose only 1.3 percent as high interest rates held back credit and building. The World Bank reports a rebound in the first half of 2026, led by investment, mining and construction, with gold exports and tourism earnings rising fast.

growth_story.tension: The sources call this one of Latin America's fastest-growing economies and cite a two-decade average for total output that is well above the 3.7 percent a year that income per person grew from 2006 to 2025; much of the difference is population growth. The data also show a slowdown the sources' long-run framing does not stress: income per person grew 4.1 percent a year in 2006 to 2015 but 3.3 percent in 2016 to 2025, with 2023 and 2025 both at 1.3 percent.
